title: Recognized in Jerusalem, Confronting Peter at Antioch
summary: Paul tells of a visit to Jerusalem where the leading apostles, James, Peter, and John, recognized his gospel and his mission to the Gentiles and did not require his Greek companion Titus to be circumcised. He then describes how he publicly opposed Peter at Antioch when Peter withdrew from eating with Gentile believers. The chapter ends with the first full statement of the letter's thesis: a person is justified not by works of the law but by faith in Jesus Christ.
story: In chapter 1 Paul insisted that his gospel came by revelation from Jesus Christ, not from any human teacher, and that he had only limited contact with the Jerusalem apostles in his early years. Chapter 2 finishes that defense with two scenes. In the first, the Jerusalem leaders examine his message and add nothing to it, a public sign that Paul and the pillars preach one gospel. In the second, Paul has to hold even Peter to that gospel when fear of a faction pulls him back from table fellowship with Gentiles. The Galatian churches were being told that Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong fully to God's people. By telling these stories Paul shows that the issue had already been settled in principle, and that backing away from it, even by an apostle, is a departure from the truth of the gospel. From here the letter moves from Paul's own story to argument from Scripture in chapter 3.
historical:
Galatians is usually dated between the late 40s and mid-50s AD, depending on how its events line up with the book of Acts. The visit of 2:1-10 came fourteen years after either Paul's conversion or his first Jerusalem visit. Scholars disagree about which visit in Acts this is. Many identify it with the Jerusalem council of Acts 15 (around AD 49), where the same question of circumcision for Gentiles was debated and the same people appear. Others identify it with the famine relief visit of Acts 11:27-30, which would explain why Paul mentions a private meeting and a request to remember the poor but says nothing about the council's letter; on this view Galatians was written before the council, making it perhaps the earliest of Paul's letters. Both views are held by careful scholars.

Antioch, on the Orontes River in Syria, was one of the largest cities of the eastern Roman Empire and the home of the first church with many Gentile members (Acts 11:19-26). It was from Antioch that Paul and Barnabas had been sent out on their first missionary trip. The men who came from James were connected to the Jerusalem church, which James the brother of Jesus led. In these years Jewish nationalism in Judea was growing, and Jews who were seen to compromise with Gentiles could face pressure, which may help explain the fear of the circumcision group that Paul describes.
cultural:
Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17) and a defining mark of Jewish identity. For many Jewish believers in Jesus it seemed obvious that Gentiles joining Israel's Messiah should take on that sign, as converts to Judaism did. Titus, a Greek (that is, a Gentile), was a test case: if the Jerusalem leaders did not require his circumcision, Gentiles could belong without it.

Meals mattered as much as circumcision. In the ancient world eating together expressed kinship and acceptance, and Jewish food laws and concerns about purity often kept observant Jews from sharing ordinary meals with Gentiles. When Peter ate with Gentile believers he was treating them as full family members; when he withdrew, the message was that they were second-class unless they became Jews. The phrase Gentile “sinners” in verse 15 reflects common Jewish usage, in which Gentiles, living outside the law, were sinners by definition. Paul quotes that assumption in order to overturn it. The right hand of fellowship (v. 9) was a public gesture of agreement and partnership.
literary: The chapter has two narrative scenes followed by a compact argument. Verses 1 to 10 are told in careful, almost legal language, as if Paul were giving testimony: who went, why, who was present, and what was agreed. Verses 11 to 14 turn sharp and direct, ending with Paul's public question to Peter. Scholars debate where Paul's words to Peter end; verses 15 to 21 may continue that speech or may be Paul now addressing the Galatians, and the passage works as a bridge between the story and the letter's main argument. The repeated contrast is between works of the law and faith in Christ, stated three times in verse 16. The chapter reaches its climax in the intensely personal verse 20 and ends with a stark conclusion in verse 21: if righteousness comes through the law, Christ died for nothing.

outline.t: Paul goes up to Jerusalem; Titus is not compelled to be circumcised
The pillars recognize Paul's gospel and mission to the Gentiles
Justified by faith in Christ, not by works of the law

doctrines.note: Verse 16 states the heart of the letter: a person is justified, declared right with God, not by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. Jewish believers who had the law had to come to Christ in the same way as Gentiles, which removes any ground for ranking believers by their heritage.

The gospel has a social shape. Peter's withdrawal from Gentile tables was, in Paul's view, not merely bad manners but a failure to walk in line with the truth of the gospel. Those justified in the same way belong at the same table.
Christ “loved me and gave Himself up for me” (v. 20). Paul's whole argument rests on the cross: if right standing with God came through the law, Christ's death would have been pointless (v. 21).

words.note: Dikaioo, to justify, to declare or show to be in the right. The word belongs to the law court: a judge justifies someone by ruling in their favor. It appears four times in verses 16 and 17. Paul uses it for God's verdict that a person is right with him, received through faith in Christ. Christians have debated how that verdict relates to the new life that follows, but in this chapter the point is how one is counted among God's righteous people.

Nomos, law. In Galatians it almost always means the law of Moses, the commands given to Israel at Sinai, including circumcision, food laws, and the Sabbath. Scholars debate whether the phrase works of the law refers to the law's commands in general or especially to those that marked Jews off from Gentiles; in context both are in view, and the dispute at Antioch was over exactly those markers.

Pistis, faith, trust, or faithfulness. Paul contrasts it with works of the law as the way a person is justified. The phrase in verses 16 and 20 can be read as faith in Christ (the believer trusting him) or as the faithfulness of Christ (his own faithful obedience to death); the Greek allows both. Most translations, including the BSB, choose faith in Christ, while a significant group of scholars favors the other reading.

Sustauroomai, to be crucified with. Paul uses it in verse 20 for the believer's union with Christ in his death: the old self, which lived under the law and for itself, has died with him. The same word is used in the Gospels for the men literally crucified with Jesus.

christ: This chapter shows Christ as the one through whom, and only through whom, anyone is justified before God, Jew or Gentile. It also shows him as a personal Savior: “the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself up for me” (v. 20). Paul describes the believer's life as Christ living in him, a union so close that Christ's death becomes Paul's death to the old way of life and Christ's life becomes his new life. And it shows that Christ's death is decisive. If a person could become right with God by keeping the law, then the cross would have been unnecessary; Paul's conclusion is that it was not, because the cross accomplished what the law never could.

hard.q: Did Paul reject the law of Moses and Jewish identity altogether?
hard.a:
Galatians can sound as if Paul dismisses the law entirely, and it has sometimes been read to cast Judaism as a religion of earning salvation by works. Many scholars in the late twentieth century, associated with what is called the New Perspective on Paul (E. P. Sanders, James Dunn, and N. T. Wright are often named), argued that first-century Judaism understood itself as a religion of grace, in which God chose Israel first and the law was the way to remain within his covenant. On their reading, Paul's quarrel in Galatians is mainly with requiring Gentiles to take on Jewish identity markers in order to belong to God's people. Defenders of the older Reformation reading reply that Paul still insists no one can be justified by doing what the law requires (v. 16), which goes deeper than ethnic markers to the human inability to be righteous before God.

Both readings agree that Paul, himself a Jew, never rejects Israel's Scriptures or Israel's God. His point is that since the Messiah has come, the law is not the way into God's people, for Jews or for Gentiles. The confrontation with Peter was about the meaning of the gospel, not an attack on Jewish people.

questions: Peter knew the truth about Gentile believers but acted against it out of fear of what others would think. Where are you tempted to let fear of a group shape how you treat other believers?
Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me.” How would you explain that sentence to someone who has never read it?
What are the unwritten requirements, beyond faith in Christ, that churches sometimes place on people before they are treated as full members of the family?
